name: Beeswax and resin setting lotion

lead: Researchers at the University of Manchester analysed hair from 18 ancient Egyptian mummies and found that nine carried a gel-like coating rich in long-chain fatty acids such as palmitic and stearic acid. The team proposed it was used like a modern styling product to keep hair shaped [1][2][3].

The 2011 findings suggested styling mattered to Egyptians in life and in death, since the coating appeared on both naturally and artificially preserved bodies. Popular accounts mention beeswax and resin, but the lead researcher said the analysis showed a fat and could not identify which [1][2][3].

paras: Based on the mummies, the product was applied to hair to hold styles, possibly curls formed with metal tools. No reliable modern recipe or procedure is established by the research [2].

No safety information exists for ancient preparations, and modern reproductions have not been tested in published studies. Resins and fats on hair may cause the usual allergic or buildup concerns of any styling product.

chain: Hairstyle stays in place in life and burial
angle.text: The coating appears to have held hair in place, much as modern gels do. Researchers suggest it was used in daily life as well as in preparing bodies for burial [2][3].

lead: The beeswax and resin setting lotion is a popular name for the hair-styling coating found on ancient Egyptian mummies. In life it would have held hair in set styles, giving a groomed look; in death the same style was kept for the afterlife [1][2].

A 2011 study led by Natalie McCreesh at the University of Manchester's KNH Centre for Biomedical Egyptology analysed 18 mummies, 15 of them from the Dakhleh Oasis cemetery dating to around 300 BCE. Nine had a gel-like substance in their hair, and gas chromatography found fatty acids [2][3].

Beeswax was considered a candidate because it contains palmitic acid, but McCreesh reported no evidence of beeswax and said the coating was a fat of unidentified type [1]. Some hair was covered with a harder, resin-like material [1].

paras: The 2011 paper in the Journal of Archaeological Science described hair from mummies of both sexes and a range of ages, including some from museum collections [1][2]. The hair carried no embalming chemicals, which the team took to mean it was protected during mummification and styled afterwards [3].

Chemical analysis identified biological fatty acids. Beeswax and resin appear in popular summaries, but the researchers did not confirm either, and the paper describes the term hair gel as a modern analogy [1].

Hairstyles in the sample ranged from long to short, and the team suggested metal curling tools might have been used with the gel holding curls [3]. Naturally dried bodies also carried it, indicating use in everyday life [1][3].
